numberItems.stem: You come to a **passive** railroad crossing. What does that mean?
options: Flashing red lights will warn you when a train is coming
There is no traffic control device — the decision to stop or go is entirely yours
Gates will lower across the road when a train approaches
numberItems.explanation: A passive crossing has no traffic control device; you must recognize the crossing, search for trains and decide if it is safe to cross (p. 2-35).

numberItems.stem: Which of these is an **active** railroad crossing?
options: One with only a crossbuck sign
One with only "X" and "RR" pavement markings
One with flashing red lights (with or without bells), or lights with bells and gates
numberItems.explanation: Active crossings have a traffic control device: flashing red lights with or without bells, or flashing red lights with bells and gates (p. 2-35).

numberItems.stem: What does the railroad **advance warning sign** look like?
options: Round, black on yellow
X-shaped, white with black letters
A large "X" and "RR" painted on the road
numberItems.explanation: The advance warning sign is round and black-on-yellow; the X-shaped sign is the crossbuck and the painted X/RR is the pavement marking (p. 2-35).

numberItems.stem: Under the handbook's advance-warning-sign rule, which vehicles are required to stop at a railroad crossing?
options: Only school buses
All vehicles carrying passengers or HazMat
Only vehicles pulling trailers
numberItems.explanation: All passenger- and HazMat-carrying vehicles are required to stop (p. 2-35); a stop is also required when the cargo or the law requires it (p. 2-36).

numberItems.stem: The pavement before a crossing has a large "X" with the letters "RR." What does it mean?
options: The same as the round advance warning sign
You must always come to a full stop at the tracks
The crossing ahead has gates
numberItems.explanation: Pavement markings mean the same as the advance warning sign: slow down, look and listen, and be ready to stop (p. 2-35).

numberItems.stem: A small sign is mounted below the crossbuck at a crossing. What does it tell you?
options: The speed of trains on that line
How far it is to the nearest rail
How many tracks the road crosses
numberItems.explanation: When the road crosses more than one track, a sign below the crossbuck shows the number of tracks (p. 2-35).

numberItems.stem: You must stop at a crossing that has **no white stop line**. Where should you stop?
options: As close to the tracks as possible so you can see better
No closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail
No closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the crossbuck sign
numberItems.explanation: With no stop line, vehicles required to stop must stop no closer than 15 feet or more than 50 feet from the nearest rail of the nearest track (p. 2-35).

numberItems.stem: You haul a cargo that requires you to stop at railroad crossings. While stopping, you should:
options: Check traffic behind you, stop gradually (use a pullout lane if there is one), and turn on your 4-way flashers
Stop as close to the tracks as you can so you can see better
Stop quickly so you don't block traffic behind you
numberItems.explanation: When stopping, check for traffic behind you while stopping gradually, use a pullout lane if available, and turn on your 4-way flashers (p. 2-36).

numberItems.stem: How long does it take a typical tractor-trailer to clear a **single** track?
options: About 3 seconds
More than 15 seconds
At least 14 seconds
numberItems.explanation: A typical tractor-trailer needs at least 14 seconds to clear a single track; more than 15 seconds is the double-track figure (p. 2-36).

numberItems.stem: Traffic is backing up beyond a **double-track** crossing. Before you start across, how much time should you expect a typical tractor-trailer to need to clear it?
options: More than 15 seconds
About 14 seconds
About 3 seconds
numberItems.explanation: A typical tractor-trailer needs more than 15 seconds to clear a double track (at least 14 seconds for a single track). Never start across unless you can get all the way over (p. 2-36).

numberItems.stem: Which rig is most likely to hang up on a raised railroad crossing?
options: A tandem-axle tractor pulling a trailer with landing gear set for a tandem-axle tractor
A single-axle tractor pulling a long trailer with landing gear set for a tandem-axle tractor
A straight truck with high ground clearance
numberItems.explanation: Low-slung units and a single-axle tractor pulling a long trailer whose landing gear is set for a tandem-axle tractor can get stuck on raised crossings (p. 2-36).

numberItems.stem: You got stuck on the tracks, got out, and moved away. When you call 9-1-1, what information does the handbook especially stress?
options: Your CDL number
The crossing's location, especially the DOT number if posted
The number of cars on the train
numberItems.explanation: Give the location of the crossing using all identifiable landmarks, especially the DOT number, if posted (pp. 2-36–2-37).

numberItems.stem: Which list gives the handbook's five factors for choosing a "safe" speed on a downgrade?
options: Weight, speed of traffic, steepness, time of day, weather
Engine power, length of grade, steepness, road conditions, weather
Total weight, length of grade, steepness, road conditions, weather
numberItems.explanation: Select a speed that is not too fast for the total weight of the vehicle and cargo, length and steepness of the grade, road conditions, and weather (p. 2-37).

numberItems.stem: The braking effect of the engine is greatest when:
options: The engine is near governed rpm and the transmission is in a lower gear
The engine is at idle and the transmission is in a high gear
The service brakes are applied at the same time
numberItems.explanation: Engine braking is greatest near the governed rpm with the transmission in the lower gears (p. 2-37).

numberItems.stem: On a long downgrade in the proper low gear, you apply the brakes until your speed is about how far below your "safe" speed, then release?
options: 10 mph
5 mph
15 mph
numberItems.explanation: Brake just hard enough for a definite slowdown until you are about 5 mph below your safe speed, then release (p. 2-38).

numberItems.stem: Using the proper downhill braking technique, each brake application should last about:
options: 14 seconds
15 seconds
3 seconds
numberItems.explanation: Each brake application should last about 3 seconds (p. 2-38). The 14- and 15-second figures are railroad-track clearing times.

numberItems.stem: Your "safe" speed on a downgrade is **40 mph**. Using the handbook technique, when do you brake and when do you release?
options: Brake when you reach 40 mph; release at about 35 mph
Brake when you reach 45 mph; release at about 40 mph
Hold light, steady pressure to stay at exactly 40 mph
numberItems.explanation: Don't brake until speed reaches the safe speed (40 mph), then slow to about 35 mph and release; repeat as needed (p. 2-38).
